Official Week 8 Objectives

1. Describe clinically relevant aspects of viral morphology.
2. Identify basic steps in the viral replication cycle targeted by antiviral drugs.
3. Compare DNA- and RNA-virus replication and apply it to pathology.
4. Recognize medically important DNA and RNA viruses, including COVID-19.
5. Describe modes of transmission of viral infections.
6. Discuss cellular and host immune responses to viral infections.
7. Relate laboratory diagnosis to virus structure and host-cell interactions.
8. Recognize clinical significance and histopathologic hallmarks of CMV, EBV, HSV, HPV, Rabies, Parvovirus B19, and RSV.

Slides 3-5, 14-15: What Makes a Virus a Virus?

Core definition
Virus = DNA or RNA genome + protein coat; obligate intracellular replication. The extracellular particle is the virion, which transfers the viral genome to another susceptible cell.
Slide 4. Envelope is acquired from host-cell membrane and contains phospholipids plus viral protein/glycoprotein spikes used for host-cell binding.
Slide 5. The deck's high-yield environmental distinction: envelopes are fragile; naked viruses are stable and tolerate acid, detergents, drying, and heat better.
FeatureEnvelopedNaked / non-enveloped
Outer layerHost-derived lipid membrane + viral spikesCapsid is outermost layer
Environmental stabilityFragile: acid/detergent/drying/heat sensitiveStable: relatively resistant
GI tractUsually poor survival in acid/bileBetter survival in acid/bile
Transmission emphasis in deckUsually body fluids; not fecal-oralReadily fecal-oral
ReleaseBudding or lysisLysis
Slide 15. Morphologic forms shown in the current deck include icosahedral, spherical, ovoid, bullet-shaped, filamentous, and pleomorphic forms.
Handout-only enrichment: the AI handout explicitly names the capsid and capsomeres and reviews icosahedral vs helical capsid organization. That explanation helps interpret slide 15, but the current deck does not devote a text slide to capsid architecture.

Slides 6-9: Viral Replication Cycle = Antiviral Target Map

Slide 7. General replication scheme maps attachment, entry, uncoating, transcription/replication, protein synthesis, assembly, and release to druggable steps.
Life-cycle order
Attachment → entry → uncoating → genome replication / transcription → protein synthesis → assembly / maturation → release.
Slide 8. Attachment determines tropism. The current slide gives EBV→CR2 on B cells, HIV→CD4 plus CCR5/CXCR4, Parvovirus B19→globoside/P antigen on proerythroblasts, and SARS-CoV-2→ACE2.
VirusAttachment receptor in current deckClinical logic
EBVCR2B-cell tropism
HIVCD4 + CCR5/CXCR4CD4 T cells / macrophages
Parvovirus B19Globoside (P antigen)Proerythroblast tropism
SARS-CoV-2ACE2Entry receptor emphasized again in COVID section
Handout-only enrichment: the 2029 handout adds concrete drug examples at each step (e.g., maraviroc for CCR5, enfuvirtide for fusion, amantadine for uncoating, polymerase/reverse-transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, oseltamivir for influenza release). Use those as mechanism reinforcement, but the current Thai deck itself is more general at this point.

Slides 10-13: DNA vs RNA Replication

Slide 10. Genome-to-mRNA/protein overview across major viral genome classes. Use it conceptually rather than memorizing every line from the figure.
Slide 11. Current DNA-virus rule: replication is in the nucleus. The slide lists poxvirus and HBV as exceptions, and emphasizes HBV's RNA intermediate / reverse transcriptase.
Slide 12. Current RNA-virus rule: replication is in the cytoplasm. Influenza/orthomyxovirus and retroviruses are nuclear exceptions. +RNA can function as mRNA; -RNA requires viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Replication-location rule
DNA → nucleus, except Pox (and the deck separately highlights HBV biology). RNA → cytoplasm, except influenza and retroviruses.
Source-specific nuance: the current deck says HBV “replicates in the cytoplasm” while also emphasizing its RNA intermediate and reverse transcriptase. The companion handout phrases the standard board rule as “DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus except Pox,” then treats HBV as a special reverse-transcribing DNA virus. For this note, memorize the deck’s HBV reverse-transcriptase exception biology rather than forcing it into a one-line location mnemonic.
Slide 13. Influenza and rotavirus have segmented genomes. The deck emphasizes influenza A reassortment of its 8 segments as the mechanism producing pandemic strains.
Influenza
Antigenic drift = slow change → seasonal/yearly outbreaks. Antigenic shift = reassortment → potential pandemic.
Handout-only board enrichment: +ssRNA can be translated directly; -ssRNA must first be copied into +RNA and therefore needs viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase available. The handout also supplies the “negative-sense viruses bring polymerase” mnemonic, which is not on the current deck.

Slides 20-21: Transmission & Progression of Disease

Slide 20. Portal of entry includes broken skin and mucosal surfaces; inhalation examples include influenza and SARS-CoV-2. After local replication, viruses may disseminate by blood or lymph; virus in blood = viremia.
Slide 21. Clinical progression: acquisition → innate defense → incubation/amplification → prodrome → specific disease → host response → shedding/contagion → resolution or persistence/chronic disease.
Progression framework
Acquisition → primary replication → dissemination/incubation → prodrome → tissue-specific disease → immune response → shedding → resolution or persistence.

Slides 22-24, 31: How Viruses Cause Injury

Slide 22. Viruses can reduce host DNA/RNA/protein synthesis, cause metabolic derangement, lysis/fusion, inclusions, neoplastic transformation, and host T-cell-mediated injury.

Direct cytopathic patterns

Slide 23. Current deck histopathology framework: syncytia, chromatin margination, inclusion bodies, and koilocytosis.
PatternViruses named in current deck
SyncytiumHSV, VZV, HIV, RSV, SARS-CoV-2
Chromatin marginationParvovirus B19, HSV, adenovirus
Inclusion bodiesLocation/staining can be diagnostic
KoilocytosisHPV

Immune-mediated injury

Slide 31. The lecture explicitly links viral disease to immunopathology: interferon/cytokines in influenza, delayed T-cell responses in measles/mumps, immune-complex mechanisms with hepatitis viruses, and immunosuppression in HIV.
Handout-only enrichment: the 2029 notes organize infection patterns as acute, chronic, and latent, and summarize interferons, NK cells, neutralizing antibodies, and CD8 T cells. That framework helps LO 6, but the current deck gives less dedicated text to these categories.

Objective gap: EBV. The official objective asks for EBV histopathologic recognition, but the current deck does not show a dedicated EBV histology image. The matching 2029 handout adds atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) in peripheral blood as its EBV recognition clue. Keep that labeled as handout enrichment rather than pretending it was shown in the current slide deck.
Handout-only diagnostic enrichment: the AI notes add PCR for viral nucleic acid, antigen testing, and serology (IgM vs IgG) as a general lab-diagnosis framework. The current deck's LO includes lab diagnosis, but it does not provide a dedicated general diagnostic-methods slide sequence.

Slides 35-45, 48: SARS-CoV-2 / COVID-19

Slide 36. Admission CXR in the lecture case shows bilateral multifocal patchy ground-glass opacities.
Slide 40. Lecture pathogenesis model: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2; loss of ACE2 function is presented as increasing Ang II, contributing to vasoconstriction, coagulopathy, alveolar damage, and respiratory failure.
Use this as the lecture model: SARS-CoV-2 → ACE2 binding / loss of ACE2 activity → ↑ Ang II → vascular and inflammatory injury → ARDS / myocardial injury / renal failure. This companion is preserving the current lecture's causal framing rather than substituting an outside mechanism.
Slide 41. SARS-CoV-2 life-cycle figure: ACE2 binding/entry, RNA release, translation, RNA replication, ER-Golgi assembly, and particle release.
Slide 42. COVID-19 pathogenesis diagram connects direct target-cell damage, innate/adaptive responses, cytokine storm/ROS/RNS, immunosuppression/secondary infection, and multiorgan dysfunction.
Slide 44. Expanded ACE2/RAAS schematic used by the lecture to explain loss of protective ACE2 signaling during infection.

Last 60 seconds
Envelope predicts stability/transmission. Genome predicts replication strategy. Receptor predicts tropism. Viral proteins + host immunity predict injury. Histology gives the buzzword diagnosis.
